Tutorial

This page is a guided Angular tutorial for building one complete feature with from the ground up. You will move step by step from project setup, to Feature State definition, to service registration, and finally to a working UI that reads and displays State through Angular-native patterns.

By the end of the page, you will have a typed , an Angular service that owns the Feature boundary, a component that binds to reactive State, and a focused detail view that renders a single character from a managed collection.

Business Use Case
  • A product team needs a simple detail view that presents one record from a managed collection without exposing state-management mechanics in the component.
  • The feature must keep domain ownership in a service so UI code can stay focused on display logic, template binding, and user interaction.
  • The same structure should scale from a read-only detail screen to later workflows such as editing, validation, loading states, and testing without changing the core boundary.

Install
↑ top

Install the /angular package to add the Angular integration to your project. The package installs the core runtime and exposes the Angular providers, decorator, injector, and Signal-based State access used throughout this tutorial.

The Angular integration includes:

  • provideVault configures the application-level .
  • provideFeatureCell registers a with Angular dependency injection.
  • @ associates an Angular service with its registered .
  • injectVault provides the registered to its Angular service.
  • state (StateSnapshotShape) exposes Signal-based access to the current State:
    • this.vault.state.value()
    • this.vault.state.error()
    • this.vault.state.isLoading()
    • this.vault.state.hasValue()

Define Feature State
↑ top

State is the feature-owned data that describes a feature at a specific moment. Defining State means deciding which values belong to the feature, assigning a type to each value, and identifying which properties are required.

In TypeScript, an interface captures those decisions as a compile-time contract for the FeatureCell and its consumers. This contract makes the expected State shape explicit, keeps State usage consistent, and allows TypeScript to identify missing properties and incompatible values during development. The interface defines the shape of State; it does not create or load a State value.

In , each declares State for a single Feature. This keeps the State definition focused on the data owned by that Feature instead of combining unrelated application data into one shared global store definition.

In this tutorial, the Feature and the State represents characters from the Star Wars universe.

Each character has an identifier, name, faction, and force-sensitive status. Keeping these fields in one focused State definition gives the , Pipeline, and Angular application a consistent representation of the character data.

Take Action
  1. Create a new file named: star-wars-character.state.ts 
{{ starWarsCharacterStateSource.source }}
Global Store vs.

In a global store, all application data is combined into one shared State definition. This can lead to a large, complex State shape that is difficult to manage and maintain. In contrast, a defines State for a single Feature, keeping the State definition focused and manageable.

Build the Angular Service
↑ top

Begin with the domain responsibility, not the integration mechanism. The character service establishes a single boundary for the Star Wars character use case and provides a stable home for the operations that will read or change character State. Its name and scope communicate what the application does, independent of how State will later be managed.

Implement that boundary as a conventional Angular service. Angular dependency injection makes the service available to consumers, while the familiar class structure keeps it focused, testable, and easy to extend. No state-management integration is required in this step; the service is ordinary Angular code organized around one application responsibility.

The initial implementation is intentionally minimal. It establishes the service’s identity and injection boundary before State behavior is added, allowing later integrations to extend a clear design rather than determine it.

Connect the Service to
↑ top

begins with the Feature, not the framework. Each establishes a deliberate domain boundary, and its service should express the use cases and State interactions that belong to that domain. Angular supplies dependency injection and lifecycle integration, but it does not define the Feature’s architecture—it is the host, not the architect.

The service remains unmistakably Angular: injectable, focused, testable, and organized around a clear application responsibility. The Angular integration for adds a thin layer of framework-native syntax, connecting the service to its through familiar decorator and injection patterns. The result is domain-led architecture expressed through conventional Angular code.

An injectable Angular service owns the interaction with the registered . The @FeatureCell decorator associates the service with the same unique key used during registration, while injectVault() provides access to its typed collection State. Exposing state from the service gives the component a read boundary built on Angular Signals, while calling initialize() activates the when Angular creates the service.

Display Character State
↑ top

This step narrows the tutorial to the UI-facing files that complete the first read path. The service boundary is already in place; now the component, template, and stylesheet turn that registered character collection into a visible detail view.

This separation is especially important in Angular because Signals, forms, and template conditions can make it tempting to move State logic into the component. Resist that. The component should coordinate the UI; the service should define the use cases that act on the registered .

In this example, the component class acts as the UI controller. It injects the service, derives one displayed character from the service's reactive State, and passes only template-ready values to the HTML view. The stylesheet is included here because it becomes the shared presentation base for the later tutorial expansions, so it is intentionally broader than this single read-only view needs by itself.
